content: The National Center for Complementary and Alternative Medicine (NCCAM) is a United States government agency that operates under the National Institutes of Health (NIH), which is part of the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS). Its primary mission is to rigorously investigate complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) practices, train researchers in this field, and provide reliable, evidence-based information to both the public and healthcare professionals. NCCAM was originally established in October 1991 as the Office of Alternative Medicine. In October 1998, it was restructured and renamed as NCCAM. The center is one of 27 institutes and centers within the NIH and is funded by Congress. It is also one of eight agencies under the Public Health Service (PHS) within the DHHS. The center focuses on four main areas: 1. Research: NCCAM funds and conducts both clinical and basic science research on CAM practices. It awards grants to researchers across the United States and internationally. Additionally, it designs and performs clinical and laboratory-based studies at the NIH campus in Bethesda, Maryland. 2. Research Training and Career Development: The center provides grants to support the training and career development of researchers at various stages, including predoctoral, postdoctoral, and established career levels. 3. Outreach: NCCAM organizes conferences, educational programs, and public exhibits. It operates an information clearinghouse to respond to inquiries and disseminates information through its website, printed publications, and town hall meetings held in various locations across the United States. 4. Integration: The center works to incorporate scientifically validated CAM practices into conventional medicine. This includes publishing research findings, studying methods to integrate evidence-based CAM into standard medical practices, and supporting programs that develop models for including CAM in the curricula of medical, dental, and nursing schools. NCCAM is structured into several divisions and offices, including: The Office of the Director The Executive Office The Division of Extramural Activities, which includes the Office of Grants Management and the Office of Scientific Review The Division of Extramural Research and Training, which includes the Office of Clinical and Regulatory Affairs, the Office of International Health Research, and the Office of Special Populations The Office of Policy, Planning, and Evaluation The Office of Communications and Public Liaison The Division of Intramural Research, which includes specialized units such as the Endocrine Section, the Diabetes Unit, and the Oncology Program Despite its efforts, NCCAM has faced criticism. Critics argue that since its inception in 1991, the center and its predecessor, the Office of Alternative Medicine, have spent over $800 million on research but have not scientifically proven the efficacy of any alternative medicine practice or declared any CAM treatment effective. Other notable aspects of NCCAM include: A multi-level peer-review process for grant applications, involving scientists, practitioners, and members of the public. Guidance and recommendations from the National Advisory Council for Complementary and Alternative Medicine, as well as from federal representatives on the Transagency CAM Coordinating Committee. A publicly accessible database, CAM on PubMed, which is a subset of the National Library of Medicine's PubMed and provides journal citations related to CAM. The NCCAM Clearinghouse, which serves as a public resource for scientifically based information on CAM and details about the center's activities. The information provided here is based on NCCAM Publication No. D158, published in June 2002, which is in the public domain.
